newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban Islamic radicals strike fear into Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban Islamic radicals strike fear into Kabul.

text.p: The radical Taleban militia that conquered Kabul last week has begun enforcing a purist brand of Islam that has struck fear into many educated people, especially women, in the Afghan capital.

The Taleban promise to govern Afghanistan, three quarters of which they control, according to Islamic Sharia law, including punishments such as death for murder, stoning for adultery and amputation for theft.
The Taleban, or religious pupils, imbibed their Sunni Moslem militancy at theological colleges set up for Afghan refugees in neighbouring Pakistan.

With Kabul firmly in their grip, the black-turbaned warriors are embarking on a daring experiment in theocracy that terrifies many residents of the capital, Afghanistan's most sophisticated and cosmopolitan city.

"We have lost our freedom," mourned a woman administrator, who asked not to be named. "The future is very dark and I don't know whether we will be able to stay in our city. The Taleban are very ignorant people."

The 33-year-old mother of three said she did not know whether she would be able to keep her job and was afraid for the future of her children, all boys, because schools have stayed shut since the Taleban conquest.

About 70 percent of teachers in Kabul are women. The Taleban's six-man interim ruling shura (council) has ordered men to report for work, but has yet to announce if and when women will be allowed to resume their jobs.

"I feel very nervous and upset," said the woman, a mathematics graduate from Kabul University. "My friends and I are Moslems, but the holy Koran only says that women must wear a scarf when they feel afraid, not all the time.

"It says both men and women should know God, which means they should be educated, otherwise how can they read the Koran and the sayings of the Prophet (Mohammad)?" she asked, twisting her fingers in anxiety.
The acting leader of the Kabul shura, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, said last week that the Taleban favour education for girls, but said it must be "within an Islamic framework".

In other Taleban areas, some girls' primary schools are open, but girls have been kept out of secondary and university education. Women in some Taleban-held areas have been allowed to work in health and education, but are not permitted to work alongside men.

The Taleban movement, whose theology has much is common with the strict Wahabi creed of Saudi Arabia, has ordered men to grow untrimmed beards within six weeks or face "severe punishment" and to wear Afghan dress.
Taleban fighters have been confiscating music cassettes from motorists and witnesses say they have beaten several men and women in the streets for violating Islamic dress codes.

The new strictures are an attempt to alter the character of Kabul, where many men are clean-shaven and wear Western clothes, and the sight of unveiled women wearing lipstick, jeans and high heels was once commonplace.

Afghanistan was declared an Islamic state after Moslem mujahideen guerrillas overthrew a Soviet-backed regime in April 1992, but the former government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani maintained a relatively tolerant atmosphere, allowing cinema, music, television and sports.

It clamped down a few months ago after Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, an Islamic radical once opposed to Rabbani, brought his Hezb-i-Islami faction back into the government and resumed his post as prime minister under a peace deal.

The Taleban gave a brutal signal of their intentions when they snatched former communist president Najibullah and his brother from a U.N. compound where they had spent more than four years and hanged them outside the presidential palace only hours after Kabul had fallen.
For the capital's beleaguered intelligentsia, the Taleban pose a far more frightening threat to their way of life.
"My daughter is in her fourth year of medical studies at Kabul University," said one employee of a foreign relief agency. "Now she cannot continue. It is a disaster."
Taleban leaders often refuse to speak to women and cannot tolerate their presence in the same room.
"What are these foreigners doing here, especially this woman?" raged Mullah Turabi at a military base visited by Western reporters on Monday.
Turabi, who has lost one eye and one leg, is the head of a new commission set up to govern Kabul.
Turabi, who is from the southern city of Kandahar where the Taleban has its headquarters, pushed and slapped a middle-ranking Taleban commander who had earlier agreed to be interviewed and filmed.
